title: The Last Crossing of Greyhaven
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Kapanmak üzere olan bir kara yolunun ucundaki eski kıyı istasyonundan on sekiz arşiv kutusunu çıkarmaya giden Mara, listede olmayan defterlerle ve baskı kalıplarıyla karşılaşır. Plan bozulup saatler daraldığında neyi taşıyacağına, geride kalanların hesabını kimin vereceğine karar vermesi gerekir.
paragraphs: ## 1. Eighteen cases

The transport sheet allowed three lines for difficulties. Mara had filled the first with 'restricted access', the second with 'fragile material', and the third with 'departure subject to crossing control'. There was no fourth line, so she had stopped thinking in categories. She checked the van's fuel, the straps, the weatherproof containers, and the telephone numbers printed beneath the regional library's logo. In the passenger seat, Nessa was eating a pear over a folded map. She had removed the map from its plastic cover because the cover made a useful plate.

'You know we have a table at the office,' Mara said. Nessa nodded, inspecting a bruise on the fruit. 'I also know you would have left without me.' This was probably true. Mara had coordinated the transfer for six weeks, and the final journey had acquired the strange importance of a last sentence. Eighteen cases from the former coastal observation station at Greyhaven, delivered to the regional library before the access road closed for rebuilding. Each case had a number, a destination shelf, and a weight. She wanted the day to end with eighteen ticks.

Greyhaven was not an island, although people across the bay called it one. A low strip of land joined it to the mainland, and a controlled road followed that strip between water and grass. Beyond it rose a broad, uneven headland with a few houses, a boatyard, and the station. The road was due to close for the winter after an inspection that afternoon. Residents had already made their own arrangements; some had moved temporarily, while others would use the licensed passenger boat. The archive was among the last loads authorised to leave by road.

At the crossing office, the controller leaned through the van window and read their permit. 'Outbound by three forty,' she said. 'That is the present limit, not a guarantee. If we change it, Ruth at the station receives the message.' Mara repeated the time and the contact name. The woman looked satisfied and lifted the barrier. As they drove onto the narrow road, the van's reflection broke into pieces in the channels beside it. Nessa put the pear core into a paper bag and began watching the water.

Mara had grown up inland, where a road generally remained a road until someone dug it up. Here, it seemed more like an agreement renewed each morning. She kept her eyes on the marked lane and drove without speaking. Far ahead, a man on a bicycle waited at the headland checkpoint. He had a yellow waterproof folded over the handlebars. As they approached, he raised one hand, then pointed them towards the station. A small white building stood against the grey slope, its windows reflecting a brighter sky than the one above them.

Ruth met them at the station door with a ring of keys. She had been its caretaker, receptionist, cleaner, and unofficial guide at different times, sometimes all on the same day. Her retirement was scheduled for the following week. Beside her stood Kit, a seasonal harbour worker hired to help with the transfer. He had brought work gloves and a notebook no larger than his palm. Mara liked that. People who wrote things down were usually easier to work with than people who assured her they would remember.

Inside, eighteen archive cases stood along the corridor, exactly as promised. Nessa, the library conservator, checked the seals while Mara matched the numbers to her sheet. Through an open doorway she could see a room without furniture. Pale rectangles marked the walls where charts had hung. A clock still worked above the doorway, and its ticking seemed unnecessarily loud. Ruth noticed her looking. 'We thought about taking it down,' she said, 'but then nobody would know when to leave.' Kit laughed, though Ruth had not quite made a joke.

Case eighteen contained photographs of the station staff. The packing list described them as institutional records, but the picture visible through the protective sleeve showed four people eating chips beside a car. One had an arm over another's shoulder. Mara closed the lid carefully. She had moved collections before: court registers, theatre costumes, a cabinet of shells. Objects acquired an official dignity when they entered her paperwork. Sometimes she forgot that they had existed before the descriptions. Nessa checked the last seal and said, 'All right. Now we need Ruth's index.'
## 2. The things outside the list

Ruth's index occupied two exercise books with different coloured covers. Neither appeared on the transport sheet. Nessa had expected them because Ruth had mentioned them in a telephone conversation, but the catalogue team had understood 'index' to mean the typed list already included in the files. Ruth opened the red book. Its pages contained dates, nicknames, short accounts of arguments, and arrows connecting photographs to people whose formal names had never reached the station register. Without it, the man holding a broken umbrella in photograph sixty-one would remain 'unidentified visitor'.

'He was the electrician,' Ruth said. 'The umbrella belonged to the director. That is why everyone was laughing.' Nessa asked whether the books could travel with the collection. Ruth hesitated. 'Most of the writing is mine. Some entries are things people told me privately. I marked those pages.' She showed them small slips of green paper. Nessa proposed a temporary restriction until Ruth could review those sections with the library. She wrote the condition on a separate form and gave Ruth a copy. Mara added 'two notebooks, restricted pending review' beneath case eighteen.

It was a reasonable addition. It weighed almost nothing. Yet Mara felt the outline of the job begin to soften. 'Is there anything else the catalogue team missed?' she asked. Ruth looked towards the back window. Beyond the garden, a track descended to a low shed with a corrugated roof. 'Elian has the printing plates,' she said. 'I thought you knew.' Mara checked the list, though she knew already that there were no printing plates on it. The only metal object described was a brass nameplate, wrapped inside case three.

Kit looked up from a container handle he was tightening. 'Elian came to the planning meeting.' Ruth nodded. 'He brought photographs. Someone said the library would be interested.' Interest was not a transport instruction, but Mara could already imagine how the difference had disappeared between the meeting and this morning. She asked how many plates there were. Ruth said twelve, perhaps fourteen, and that some were quite large. Nessa asked what had been printed from them. 'The harbour notices,' Ruth answered. 'And the local maps. Before everything came from the town.'

Mara looked at the clock. It was half past ten. Loading the cases would take less than an hour; the road was twenty minutes away. There was time to inspect the plates, establish ownership, and decide whether another transfer should be arranged. She made that distinction aloud. Ruth listened without interruption, then said, 'Of course.' The polite answer made Mara feel harsher than she had intended. She asked Kit to stay with the van and the sealed cases. Nessa took a notebook, and the three women went down the track.

The shed door stood open. Inside, Elian was wrapping a flat object in an old cotton sheet. He was the cyclist from the checkpoint, older than Mara had thought, with grey hair cut close to his scalp and ink permanently lodged beside one thumbnail. The room smelled of oil and paper. A heavy printing press stood against the wall, its wheel taller than a bicycle wheel. Shelves held type, tools, and wooden trays. Elian saw Mara glance at the press and smiled. 'You can stop calculating. That stays here.'

His family had once printed notices for the station and the harbour. He still used the press for small commissions, and his house stood safely on the upper lane. He was not leaving Greyhaven. What he wanted moved were the old plates and their sample sheets, which belonged to the station under an arrangement nobody had yet located in writing. He had kept them because the station's store was damp. Now the store was empty and the collection was leaving. He wanted the plates to remain with the records that explained them.

Nessa examined one plate without touching its engraved face. It showed the headland as a series of lines: road, shore, footpaths, buildings. The station appeared solid and central. The print shop was a tiny rectangle near the edge. Elian laid a paper impression beside it. Beneath the station's formal title, someone had written local names in pencil. 'The printed version and the version people used,' he said. Mara recognised the track they had just walked, though on the official sheet it ended before reaching the shed. Beyond that point, the map was blank.
## 3. A different kind of weight

Elian had expected a larger vehicle. He had also expected a conversation about access to the collection once it left. Neither expectation seemed unreasonable, but together they made Mara feel that the van had arrived carrying the wrong promise. She explained the library's reading room arrangements as far as she knew them. Nessa added that the material would first be assessed and catalogued. Elian listened, then asked what 'first' meant in months. Neither woman could give him an honest number. Outside, a loose length of wire tapped against the shed roof.

'I am not asking for a display with my name on it,' he said. 'I am asking whether Ruth can find a page when someone rings her.' Ruth stood beside the open door, her hands deep in her cardigan pockets. She had answered questions about Greyhaven for thirty years. Transferring the archive would relieve her of unpaid work, but it would also move the answers beyond the reach of the people who still called. Mara had understood access as a road problem. Here it was becoming a question about what happened after arrival.

Nessa suggested a practical first step. The notebooks could be photographed after Ruth's private entries were separated, and a working copy returned to the local reading room. The plates could be catalogued alongside their paper impressions. She did not promise an exhibition or an immediate public website. She wrote down the actions she could actually undertake and put her own name beside them. Elian read the page twice. 'That sounds smaller than what they said at the meeting,' he observed. 'It is smaller,' Nessa replied. 'It is also something I can do.'

There were twelve plates. Six were small enough to fit into an empty container, but the others required flat support. Together with their protective boards, they were heavier than Mara wanted to guess at. Elian had a scale used for paper deliveries. They weighed the wrapped groups and recorded the figures. The van could carry the complete load within its permitted limit, and there was space along one side if the archive cases were rearranged. Mara telephoned her manager, explained the ownership uncertainty, and obtained approval for temporary deposit rather than permanent acquisition.

Ruth produced a station ledger showing that the plates had been paid for from its printing account. That did not settle every possible question, but it supported taking them into documented temporary care. Nessa photographed the relevant page and prepared a receipt naming Elian as their present custodian. Mara wrote the additional weight on her sheet. It extended beyond the little box provided. For the first time that morning, she found the untidy margin reassuring. A number outside a box was still a number; an unwritten assumption was harder to carry responsibly.

While Nessa packed the smaller plates, Elian showed Mara a narrow green volume. It contained the corrections made to successive map printings. A footpath had moved because a wall fell. A landing had changed its name because boats stopped using the older one. Each alteration included a date and, sometimes, a short explanation. The book belonged with the plates, he said, but he wanted a copy. Mara added it to the receipt. She also noticed a photograph tucked inside the cover: a young woman beside the press, laughing at something beyond the frame.

Elian saw her pause. 'My sister. She ran this place before I did.' He removed the photograph and put it in his shirt pocket. Mara was grateful that he had made the decision himself. There was a particular discomfort in watching people decide, under the pressure of a collection visit, which parts of their lives counted as personal and which might become useful history. She had no wish to turn his hesitation into a donation. Nessa finished the final wrapper and asked him to check the written description of every item.

By noon, the plates were ready for the van. Kit arrived with the first of two low trolleys, sent by Ruth to help. They loaded only what each trolley was designed to carry, leaving the remaining groups on the shed's sturdy table. The route uphill was short but steep, and progress required more patience than strength. Halfway to the station, Mara stopped to change hands. From there, she could see the crossing road and the mainland roofs beyond it. The distance looked manageable. She would remember that impression later with considerable irritation.
## 4. The road closes early

They had loaded half the archive when Kit noticed liquid beneath the van. He did not touch it. He called Mara over, and she saw a thin dark line spreading from inside the front wheel. Nothing in her transport training authorised her to diagnose it by appearance. She rang the fleet service, described the position, and sent photographs. The mechanic asked several questions, then told her not to drive. A recovery vehicle would have to come from the mainland. Mara looked at the remaining cases in the corridor and asked for an arrival estimate.

The answer was at least two hours. She called the crossing office before she called her manager. The controller remembered the van and sounded distracted. An inspection team was reporting deterioration along the road edge. All authorised traffic was being brought forward. Outbound vehicles already on the headland would be directed across by one thirty; after that the barrier would close until the engineers decided otherwise. The controller could not admit a recovery truck on the chance that it might return before the closure. The van would have to remain at the station.

For a few seconds, Mara watched Kit tighten the cap on his water bottle. She could hear herself explaining that they had a permit, that the transfer had been booked for weeks, that the cases were loaded. None of those statements changed a damaged road. She stopped before saying the third. 'Understood,' she told the controller. 'We will not attempt to move the van. Can you confirm the passenger boat arrangements?' The woman gave her the harbour office number and asked her to keep the station telephone free for further instructions.

The boat was still operating between the sheltered inner landing and the mainland harbour. Its skipper, Ivo, had one scheduled afternoon departure and could take the team, subject to the harbour's conditions. Cargo required separate discussion. Mara knew him from the backup section of her plan, which had consisted of his telephone number and the word 'possible'. When he answered, she wished she had asked more useful questions six weeks earlier. He listened to the list, then asked for weights, dimensions, passenger numbers, and the exact loading point. She could answer only three of those immediately.

The station's nearest landing was no longer in use for passenger boarding. The authorised inner landing lay on the other side of the headland. A service lane reached it, but the van was the only available vehicle large enough for the cases. Ivo could not simply bring the boat to the beach below the station. He explained this without apology, and Mara found that she preferred his certainty to encouraging possibilities. He would speak to the harbour supervisor about additional cargo. She should send him the figures and wait for a definite answer.

Nessa was standing beside case nine when Mara returned to the corridor. 'We have a road problem,' Mara said. 'And a vehicle problem. They have unfortunately decided to cooperate.' Kit gave a brief laugh. Ruth did not. She asked whether everyone was safe, and Mara said yes. The cases were dry, the building remained secure, and the road closure did not mean the headland itself was being evacuated. Those facts helped settle the room. They were facing a failed transport plan, not a command to abandon judgement.

Ruth made sandwiches while Mara called the library. Her manager first suggested hiring another van, then understood the closure and stopped suggesting things from a distance. He authorised secure temporary storage at the station if the material could not travel. The collection could be moved later by a properly arranged boat service. That option was real, and Mara wrote it at the top of a fresh page. It prevented every later choice from becoming a false contest between immediate removal and total loss. The station would still have locks and a roof tomorrow.

Yet some material needed attention soon. Nessa had identified damp inside three cases despite their recent packing. The plates and their paper samples were now out of Elian's controlled workshop, though they could return there if necessary. The library had prepared a treatment space and staff for the following day. Moving the vulnerable items would be useful; moving everything merely to complete Mara's sheet would not. She crossed out the word 'complete' in her private notes and replaced it with 'appropriate'. It was an ungainly word, but it asked a better question.
## 5. What can travel

Ivo called at one fifteen. The harbour had authorised a cargo allocation on the afternoon boat, but only within a defined weight and deck arrangement. Four passengers could accompany it. Elian would stay in Greyhaven, as planned, and would help until loading. The boat had sufficient capacity for the selected load; the limiting issue was the combination of size, secure stowage, and the time available to bring it down. Ivo would inspect everything before accepting it. Departure was scheduled for five twenty from the inner landing. He would contact them if conditions changed.

Mara repeated the details while Kit wrote them on the whiteboard. They had four hours, two trolleys, several sets of hands, and a route nobody in the room had yet checked for this load. Elian knew a pedestrian way shorter than the service lane. Part of it followed the old tramway used by the print shop. There were gates, a narrow bridge over a drainage ditch, and a section where the trolleys would need to be unloaded. It was possible, he said, but possible was not the same as quick. Mara asked him to walk it with Kit first.

While they were gone, Nessa opened the packing records. The eighteen cases had been arranged by subject, not by urgency or whether another copy existed. Six held printed reports already digitised and available at the library. Four held unique registers. Three contained the damp material. The others held photographs, correspondence, and equipment records. The plates were a separate addition, requiring careful support. Mara could see why the original tidy numbering was now unhelpful. Case one was first because its subject began earliest in the catalogue, not because it should move first.

They made three groups: material needing prompt attention, unique material ready to travel, and stable material that could remain securely until a later collection. Nessa explained each decision, and Ruth checked whether a supposedly duplicate report contained handwritten additions. Twice, it did. Those pages were recorded and moved into a suitable protective folder with a cross-reference left behind. Nothing was discarded. The aim was to reduce the immediate load without breaking the connections that made the papers understandable. Mara found herself listening to Nessa's descriptions with the concentration she usually reserved for road instructions.

The map plates caused the longest discussion. They were heavy, awkward, and stable in Elian's workshop. Taking them today would consume space that could carry more papers. Elian had not yet returned, so Mara resisted the temptation to make the decision for him. They could propose leaving the plates under the temporary deposit agreement until a dedicated transfer was arranged. Their paper impressions and correction book could accompany the archive now. The objects would remain connected through their records even while they occupied different places. Nessa wrote a clear proposal instead of quietly removing them from the list.

Ruth sat at the table, turning the red index book over in her hands. 'It feels as though we are choosing which things matter,' she said. Nessa put down her pencil. 'We are choosing which things need this journey today.' She showed Ruth the future collection column, including dates by which the library would contact Elian and the station owner. A column could become another empty promise, Mara knew. She added the name of the person responsible for each action, including her own. Then she sent the revised plan to her manager and requested written acknowledgement.

Kit and Elian returned shortly before two. The shorter route was passable, but a gate beside the boatyard was locked. Elian knew the owner and had already arranged to borrow the key. The drainage bridge was sound and open to pedestrians, but too narrow for the wide trolley. They would carry individual containers across and reload on the other side. Kit had measured the opening rather than relying on his impression. He drew the difficult section on the whiteboard. For the first time since the phone call, the afternoon had a shape they could discuss.

Elian accepted the proposal about the plates after reading it in silence. He asked for one change: the library should collect them from his workshop, not expect him to bring them to a landing. Mara added that condition. He took the receipt, folded it carefully, and said he would help return the plates before joining the carrying team. Their combined load was now smaller, properly documented, and still substantial. Mara sent the final weights and dimensions to Ivo. His reply arrived while they were repacking: 'Received. Bring only this list. Call before leaving the station.'
## 6. The borrowed key

Mara rang Ivo from the station doorway at twenty-five past two, because he had asked her to and because his instruction was the only fixed point the afternoon had so far produced. 'We are leaving now,' she said. 'Then I shall see you when I see you,' said Ivo. 'Mind the bridge. People forget the bridge until they are standing on it.' She had not mentioned a bridge. She decided that this was not a puzzle worth spending battery on.

The nine cases from the van came out first. The van had been loaded in numerical order, which had seemed sensible at nine o'clock and now meant that the day's two groups were shuffled together like cards. Three of the nine were going, and seven more were waiting in the corridor. Kit marked all ten on the end with a yellow cross of chalk, a sign that meant nothing to anyone outside the five of them, and Mara noticed that she trusted it more than the printed numbers. The six that were staying went back beside the two that had never left. Nessa covered all eight with plastic sheet, tucked a card under each giving the number, the contents and Mara's name, and stood back like someone leaving a ward for the night.

Ruth locked the station door and tried the handle twice. Through the glass, the clock above the doorway went on ticking over the shapes under their sheets. She did not look at it again, and Mara, who noticed, understood that this was a decision and not an oversight.

The old tramway began behind the shed, where the track from the station ran out of surface and became cinders. Two iron rails still lay in it, worn bright on top and brown at the sides, and for the first hundred metres the wheels of both trolleys wanted to follow them. Kit had walked the route out and back that afternoon and took command of it without being asked. He counted aloud in fives. At two hundred paces everyone stopped. At four hundred they stopped again, whether or not anyone needed to. 'Rest before you need it,' he said. 'It's cheaper.' He said it like a proverb, and by the third stop Mara was prepared to treat it as one.

Elian caught them up at the first bend, wheeling his bicycle. The plates were back under their sheets in the shed, he reported, and the shed was padlocked, which was more than could be said for it in forty years. He took the case Mara had insisted on carrying out of her hands without negotiation, and she let him, although her fingers stayed curled around the shape of the handle for some time afterwards.

At the second rest nobody sat on a case; that was Nessa's single rule. Ruth sat on a boundary stone instead, with the red notebook in a bag across her chest and her chin lifted towards the water. 'Thirty years I have known this path,' she said, 'and I never saw it closed. I never saw it formally opened, either.' Elian, who had pushed barrows down it as a boy, pointed along the cinders. 'Paper came up this way. Paper, then ink, then my grandfather's complaints. The tram stopped the year somebody asked what it was for.' Nobody laughed, but Kit wrote it down.

Where the boatyard wall closed in on their left, the route stopped being a route and became a set of sensations: the trolley strap across Mara's shoulder, the cold of a handle through her glove, the dull arithmetic of another two hundred. It ended at a double gate of green planks, chained and padlocked, and leadership passed to Elian without announcement. 'This is where I become useful,' he said. He took from his pocket a key on a loop of tarred twine and a note the yard's owner had left that morning, written in capitals. KEEP IT LOCKED. NOTHING NEAR THE CRADLES. THE KEY COMES BACK TO THE HOUSE, NOT THE OFFICE. 'She is a reasonable woman,' he said, 'who dislikes being surprised.' He opened the padlock, held the gate while the trolleys went through and, when the last of them was in, threaded the chain from the inside and snapped the lock shut again, because the note said so. Then he put the key back in the pocket where he kept his sister's photograph.

The yard smelled of paint and cold iron. Hulls stood on their cradles like patient animals with the sea taken away. Elian led them along a line of whitewashed stones that kept clear of the winch cables, and nobody spoke until they reached the far fence, where the ground fell into a drainage ditch and a single bridge of plank and concrete crossed it, with an iron handrail on one side only.

Kit measured it again, as if the number might have changed in his absence. 'Seventy-one centimetres,' he said. 'The wide trolley is seventy-eight. I would have preferred to be wrong.' The trolleys went over first, empty and folded, like stretchers. Then Nessa took charge of the bridge as naturally as she had taken charge of the seals. One case at a time; one person on the bridge; the receiver on the far side with both hands free before the carrier set off. Nobody was to speak to the carrier. 'Not because it is dramatic,' she said. 'Because the only thing that can go wrong is somebody turning their head.'

At the far end Kit read each chalk cross, then the number beneath it, and wrote the number down. Mara carried number thirteen herself, one of the damp three, eighteen kilograms of paper that smelled of cellars. Halfway across she made the mistake of looking up. Beyond the fence, beyond the quay lane and the water, the mainland roofs sat in a tidy row. The distance looked manageable. She noted, with something close to gratitude, that the irritation she had been promised had arrived exactly on time.

It took thirty-five minutes. Ruth went over with the notebooks and the folders, Nessa last, and when the final case had come off the bridge Kit read the count aloud: ten crosses, ten numbers, no gaps. Mara wrote it on her sheet. Nobody cheered. Kit's knuckles had gone raw, so along the quay lane Mara took the front and counted in fives, because it was cheaper. It was twenty past four when the lane ended at the water.
## 7. Contents, not numbers

The inner landing was not a place anyone would have chosen to hurry. A granite quay curved round a pool of dark water like a hand cupped to keep something in, and Ivo's boat lay against a pontoon at the bottom of a ramp: a stubby white launch with a green wheelhouse and the name Gannet in plain letters. The tide was out. At high water the ramp was a gentle slope; now it dropped to the pontoon at the angle of a ladder, its boards slick and green.

Kit looked down it and said something that his notebook did not record. The trolleys had been the plan: down the ramp, along the pontoon, alongside the boat. The ramp had been built for a different tide. Ivo, who stood on the pontoon in a navy hat with a clipboard under his arm, offered no opinion. He pointed instead to a hand davit bolted to the edge of the quay, a rusted arm with a crank, used for lobster pots and outboard engines. Kit, to Mara's lasting gratitude, knew exactly how it worked.

'Each case goes into the sling and is weighed in the air,' said Ivo, who had already shackled a brass-faced hook scale into the davit's line. 'Then it comes down to me. You read me the number; I read you the weight.' He was a broad man in his sixties, whose timetable was set by the water and not by anybody's anxiety. 'The limit is two hundred kilograms on that foredeck, passengers not included. It is not an opinion.' Mara took the list from her folder. It said a hundred and ninety-four, a figure he had accepted that afternoon in a single short message.

The scale, older than Mara, took each case with a small shudder and settled. Kit read the chalk and the number, Mara found the line on the list, and Ivo said the weight. Eighteen, said the list, and Mara thought of her shoulder; twenty-one, said Ivo. Sixteen; seventeen. At the end the figure on his pad was two hundred and seven. The three damp cases had drunk eleven kilograms between them since the packers' scales, and straps and polythene had added the rest.

'Seven over,' said Ivo, not unkindly. 'I can take a hundred and ninety-four on a list I have accepted, or two hundred on a deck I have measured. I cannot take two hundred and seven on a hope.' Mara heard herself begin: the permit, the six weeks, the bridge. She stopped at the first clause, as she had stopped that morning with the controller. None of it altered a deck rating.

She looked at the sheet. It held numbers, destination shelves and weights. It could not tell her what any case was for. 'Which seven kilos?' asked Kit. The sheet said what the packers had believed six weeks ago, and the catalogue team had believed, in the same spirit, that an index was a typed list. 'Nessa,' Mara said, 'I need what is in them. Not what they are called.' Nessa already had a thumbnail under the first seal. 'Ten minutes,' she said. 'We have thirty,' said Ivo, 'and the bar will not wait for a tidy list.' Mara could hear the minutes she did not have being spent. She said, 'Go on.'

They did it on the pontoon, as the bridge had taught them: one case at a time, one voice. Kit read the number; Mara said what her sheet promised; Nessa lifted the lid a hand's width and said what was there. A register, as promised. Photographs in sleeves, as promised. A bundle of correspondence tied with grey tape. Time after time the lid agreed with the list, and each time Mara drew a tick and felt the pen slow in her hand, because a tick written in a hurry was only a belief with a mark beside it.

Case fourteen was listed as a register, 1921 to 1934, unique, twenty-three kilograms. Nessa raised the lid and stopped. The register lay there in its tissue, but beneath it was a thick layer of printed bulletins, laid flat to stop the volume sliding. 'Duplicates,' she said, fanning a corner. 'The annual bulletins, the same as in cases two and seven, and those are staying. Five kilos at least. Someone wanted it not to rattle.' 'Thirty years of lists,' said Ivo, 'and not one of them has been wrong in a convenient direction. Take it as a gift, and do not expect another.'

The bulletins rose alone in the sling: five kilograms exactly, a tidy number that belonged to nobody. Nessa folded her scarf into the gap so that the register could not slide, and for the first time that day Mara saw her look undignified in the service of the collection. 'Two hundred and two,' said Ivo. 'Two over.'

The impressions had been the last addition to the list: twelve sheets of stiff card in a grey folder, four kilograms, written in Mara's margin outside the box. She did not decide. She went to where Elian was coiling a line that nobody had asked him to coil. 'They were meant to travel with the archive,' she said. 'That is what we agreed. I can leave them with you instead, until the plates go.' He looked at the folder for a long time, reading it twice, as he had read Nessa's page. 'They were printed in my shop,' he said. 'They can wait for their plates. It will do them good to be together.'

Ivo took Mara's pen, which until then had been used only for ticks. He struck out one line, corrected the weight of case fourteen, wrote a new total of a hundred and ninety-eight, and signed beneath it with the time: sixteen fifty-eight. 'Now it is a list I can carry,' he said. 'Two kilograms is not a margin. It is a rounding error. But it is an honest one.' The bulletins went into the harbour's parcel cage. Freight crossed on Thursdays in the winter, he said, every other week; the next was the twelfth, if the supervisor found deck space for plates. Nessa added a line to Elian's receipt: twelve impressions, held by Elian, to travel with the plates. The date was left blank. Mara looked at the blank for a moment and wrote her own name beside it.
## 8. The short crossing

Ivo stowed the cargo as though he were laying a table. The heaviest cases went amidships and low, against the wheelhouse, where the boat's weight already lived. The three damp ones went on slatted duckboards in the lee, where spray could not reach and air could, under a tarpaulin that Nessa lifted every few minutes. Everything was strapped. 'If I can see it move, it is not stowed,' he said. 'If I cannot see it, it is not checked. Either way it is my problem.' Mara signed the manifest where he tapped, and he countersigned. It was strange how little the signatures weighed.

By then the quay had acquired an audience. Three people had walked down from the upper lane, which was what one did for the last boat when the road was closing for the winter: a man with a spaniel, a woman carrying a flask under her arm like a baton, a boy on the wall with his heels knocking. They did not look at the cases. They looked at Ruth. 'Is it true the photographs are going?' the woman asked. 'Some of them,' said Ruth. 'The ones that need a drier room than ours. The rest are staying under sheets, and the books are going to be copied.' 'And who tells the library who is in the lifeboat picture?' 'You ring me,' said Ruth. 'Not the station. After next week that number rings in an empty corridor.' She took the boy's chalk and wrote her own number on the slate beside the ramp, in the slanted figures of someone who had written the station's on forms for thirty years and had never once been asked to write her own.

Elian stood at the head of the ramp with the yard key in his hand. Ruth took a second key from her ring and held it a moment longer than she needed to. 'The corridor light is on a timer,' she said. 'The clock wants winding on Fridays.' 'Then I shall look in on Fridays,' said Elian. 'I do not trust dates that are not written down, but I can trust a Friday.' Mara, who ought to have objected on the library's behalf, wrote the key on the receipt with her name beside it. It was not strictly within her authority, and she knew exactly whom she would have to tell, and how soon.

At twenty past five, to the minute, Ivo took in the stern line himself. He had not looked at a clock. He had looked at the water against the piles, then at the sky over the bar, then, briefly, at Mara, as if confirming that the list and the person carrying it were the same. Elian stood on the quay with his hands in his pockets, the way people stand when they have decided not to wave. Then he waved.

The crossing took twenty-five minutes. The launch slid out of the pool, past the last cradle and the harbour wall, and met the swell at the bar, which lifted it and set it down again with long, slow indifference. Mara found a place where her back could rest against a case, remembered Nessa's rule, and stood instead, holding a rail that was still cold from the afternoon. The light was going the colour of slate.

Ruth sat in the lee of the wheelhouse with the red notebook on her knees and did not open it. Nessa lowered herself beside her, took from her coat a pear that was the worse for a day of being carried, and cut it in two with a conservator's scalpel. 'You carry a scalpel for fruit,' said Ruth. 'I carry a scalpel for everything,' said Nessa. 'The fruit is the least of it.' Then she took a card from her notebook, wrote on it, and handed it over. It was a list, not a promise. A working copy of both notebooks, with the marked pages withheld, in the Greyhaven reading room by the thirtieth of November. Ruth's review of every withheld page at the library tomorrow at ten. The plate impressions photographed by the fifteenth of December, and a print left with Elian. Nessa's name beside each. Ruth read it twice.

'Put my number on it,' she said, 'not the station's. The people who ring will still be there after the desk has gone.' She turned the red book over. 'They told me those things because it was me. I should like to be asked about every one of them before anybody else decides they are history.' Nessa wrote Ruth's name and home number under her own. 'Then it is a condition,' she said, 'not a favour.'

Kit had stopped writing. 'What do you put,' he asked Mara, 'for the ones that stayed?' 'A reason, a name and a date,' she said. 'The reason has to fit in one sentence. If I cannot say it to someone who was not there, it is not a decision. It is a mood.' 'And if the date slips?' 'Then the name is the person who has to explain why.' He wrote that down too. She watched him do it and, for the first time that day, felt the ordinary pressure of being quoted.

Halfway across she turned. Greyhaven lay behind them as a long dark shape without edges, the road a faint pale thread beside it, the station a smaller darkness on the slope. Then a window lit near the shed, which was Elian's lamp, and a minute later another on the hill: the corridor light, on the timer Ruth had set with the embarrassed air of someone confessing to a superstition. It shone on eight covered cases and a clock that still knew the time. 'It costs a few pence a night,' Ruth said, to nobody. 'Somebody should find it lit.'
## 9. Ticks and names

Mara's manager had come to the harbour in person, having stopped suggesting things from a distance. He stood on the quay in a coat too good for the weather and shook Ivo's hand as though something had been agreed, which, in a way, it had. Behind him the library's own van waited with its back doors open, and beside it a registrar who had stayed late and wore the look of a person who had been told to expect a few cases. Kit tore a page from his notebook before he went to catch the last bus: the bridge count, ten numbers in a column, signed. It was the first receipt a seasonal harbour worker had ever given her.

In the loading bay, under lights that hid nothing, the registrar read the list aloud while Nessa lifted the lids, and ten cases agreed with ten lines. Mara had expected relief. What she felt was closer to the pleasant dullness of a sum that comes out right. Nobody around her used the word 'approximately'.

The treatment room had been made ready for the next morning, but two conservators came back from their dinners with their coats still on, and within the hour the damp cases lay open on the long table: interleaving tissue, blotters, a fan on its lowest setting. Two of the three would be dry and flat within the week. In case thirteen, the one Mara had carried over the bridge, the last forty pages of a ledger had fused into a single grey block. 'It was like this before it left the station,' Nessa said, which was probably true, and which Mara was grateful to be told. She would know in a month, she added, and wrote the date on the folder. From case three she lifted a brass nameplate that had left a green bloom on its wrapping, and read it aloud: GREYHAVEN COASTAL OBSERVATION STATION and, beneath, in smaller letters, ENQUIRIES TO THE CARETAKER. Ruth, on a stool by the radiator with a mug of tea she was not drinking, laughed once, quietly, and then stopped.

At half past eight Ruth and Nessa sat down with the two notebooks and a pencil and began to decide, page by page, which of them were Ruth's to give. They would not finish tonight; the card said ten o'clock tomorrow. It was the one job of the day that nobody tried to hurry.

Mara was alone with her transport sheet at nine. It looked the way an exercise book looks the evening before it is marked: careful columns, a blue pen, the optimism of the first page. Eighteen lines. She counted the ticks twice, which she had not needed to do in years. Ten. Beside the other eight she did not leave a gap. Cases one, two, four, seven, nine and twelve: printed reports, already digitised, under sheets in the station corridor, cards in place. Cases six and fifteen: equipment records, the same. For all eight the reason was written out in a line, the owner was Mara, and the day was the twelfth of November, a Thursday, on Ivo's freight crossing. She had chosen it because Ruth would still hold the keys and could sign for whatever left the building. Ruth's last day was the Friday.

Below the line, in the untidy margin she had once found reassuring, she wrote the rest. Two notebooks, restricted pending review: Nessa, with Ruth, ten o'clock tomorrow. Five kilograms of bulletins in the parcel cage: Ivo, the twelfth. Twelve plates and twelve impressions in Elian's workshop, receipt signed: the library to collect, Mara for transport, Nessa for the condition report, the twelfth. The fused ledger: Nessa, a month. Working copies for the Greyhaven reading room: Nessa, the thirtieth. The van, with its flat wheel in the station yard: the fleet service, when the engineers reopened the road, and Mara until it was gone.

Ten ticks and eight names, and at the foot of the page six lines that had not existed that morning. It was not the sentence she had wanted when she imagined eighteen ticks. It was longer than that, and every part of it was somebody's. She found, rather to her surprise, that she could read it aloud to a stranger without lowering her voice.

She rang Elian first, because he had said he did not trust dates that were not written down, and she read him the twelfth, ten o'clock, the workshop, the receipt. 'And the green book?' he asked. 'Photographed this week. Your copy comes over with us on the twelfth.' She could hear the shed behind him: wood, a settling radiator. 'I shall bring my sister's photograph out of my pocket that morning,' he said. 'Not to keep. To be copied, if somebody asks nicely. I will decide on the day.' 'That is yours to decide,' said Mara. 'Yes,' said Elian. 'I thought you would say that.'

Then she rang the harbour office, where Ivo answered on the second ring. The backup section of her plan had once consisted of his number and the word 'possible'. She read him what she had now: a date, a deck, a weight, a name beside each. 'The supervisor gave you the slot the moment I asked,' he said. 'Thursday the twelfth, ten o'clock, freight deck. Send me the list. When I have approved it, bring only what is on it, and call before you leave the station.'

quiz.q: Why do Ruth's two notebooks matter to the collection?
options: They list the weight of every case for the boat
They are the only record of the road closure
They name people and explain local context that the formal records leave out
They prove that Elian owns the printing plates

quiz.q: What stops the team from finishing the job by road?
options: The van leaks and the controller brings the closure forward
Ruth refuses to lock the station
The library cancels the transfer
Nessa decides the cases are too damp to travel

quiz.q: Why are the cases carried over the drainage bridge one at a time?
options: Ivo has asked for every case to be counted twice
The yard's owner allows only one person through at a time
The cinders are too soft for the trolleys
The bridge is too narrow for the wide trolley, and Nessa wants one careful carrier on it at a time

quiz.q: How does Mara bring the load under Ivo's two-hundred-kilogram limit?
options: She persuades Ivo to accept a few extra kilograms
She removes duplicate bulletins from one case and, with Elian's agreement, leaves the impressions with him
She leaves a passenger on the quay
She sends case fourteen back to the station

quiz.q: How does Mara's final sheet differ from the 'eighteen ticks' she wanted at the start?
options: It shows eighteen ticks after a second crossing that night
It shows no ticks, because the transport sheet was damaged
It shows ten ticks, and every other item has a named owner, a reason and a date
It shows fourteen ticks, with the plates counted as extra cases
